claim: Melanopsin signaling within intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC) subtypes impacts a broad range of behaviors from circadian photoentrainment to conscious visual perception.
source: Melanopsin signaling within intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC) subtypes impacts a broad range of behaviors from circadian photoentrainment to conscious visual perception.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge about melanopsin and ipRGCs.

claim: HCN channels are dispensable for M4 phototransduction.
source: In this study, we resolve two opposing models of M4 phototransduction, demonstrating that hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are dispensable for this process
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no reduction in M4 photocurrent when HCN channels are blocked with ZD7288 for 5-8 minutes (Figure 2B and C).

claim: M4 phototransduction involves melanopsin-dependent potassium channel closure and canonical transient receptor potential (TRPC) channel opening.
source: demonstrating that hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are dispensable for this process and providing support for a pathway involving melanopsin-dependent potassium channel closure and canonical transient receptor potential (TRPC) channel opening.
evidence: Supported by data showing TRPC3/6/7 channels contribute to the early transient component of M4 photocurrent (Figure 1C and D) and previous work on potassium channel closure.

claim: HCN channels are dispensable for M2 phototransduction.
source: Surprisingly, we find that HCN channels are likewise dispensable for M2 phototransduction, contradicting the current model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no reduction in M2 photocurrent when HCN channels are blocked with ZD7288 for 5-8 minutes (Figure 4D and E).

claim: M2 phototransduction requires TRPC channels in conjunction with T-type voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: We instead show that M2 phototransduction requires TRPC channels in conjunction with T-type voltage-gated calcium channels, identifying a novel melanopsin phototransduction target.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing TRPC3/6/7 knockout reduces M2 photocurrent by ~75% (Figure 5A and B) and T-type VGCC blockade nearly eliminates M2 photocurrent (Figure 9B and C).

claim: T-type voltage-gated calcium channels are a novel melanopsin phototransduction target in M2 ipRGCs.
source: We instead show that M2 phototransduction requires TRPC channels in conjunction with T-type voltage-gated calcium channels, identifying a novel melanopsin phototransduction target.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing T-type VGCC blockade with TTA-P2 nearly eliminates M2 photocurrent (Figure 9B and C).

claim: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain regions to influence subconscious non-image-forming functions such as circadian photoentrainment, the pupillary light reflex, learning, and mood.
source: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain regions to influence subconscious non-image-forming functions such as circadian photoentrainment, the pupillary light reflex, learning, and mood (Hattar et al., 2003; Lucas et al., 2003; Mrosovsky and Hattar, 2003; Panda et al., 2003; Altimus et al., 2008; Lupi et al., 2008; Göz et al., 2008; Gooley et al., 2012; LeGates et al., 2012; Fernandez et al., 2018; Rupp et al., 2019; Sondereker et al., 2020; Aranda and Schmidt, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: M2-M6 ipRGCs primarily innervate brain areas involved in conscious visual perception and are necessary for proper contrast sensitivity.
source: M2-M6 ipRGCs primarily innervate brain areas involved in conscious visual perception and are necessary for proper contrast sensitivity (Ecker et al., 2010; Estevez et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2023; Schmidt et al., 2014; Stabio et al., 2018; Quattrochi et al., 2019; Aranda and Schmidt, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Melanopsin phototransduction is required for intrinsic light sensitivity across ipRGC subtypes.
source: Despite diverse behavioral functions, one common feature across ipRGC subtypes is that melanopsin (Opn4) phototransduction is required for intrinsic light sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Melanopsin null mutant animals show deficits in both image-forming and non-image-forming behaviors.
source: Indeed, melanopsin null mutant animals show deficits in both image-forming and non-image-forming behaviors (Panda et al., 2002; Ruby et al., 2002; Lucas et al., 2003; Schmidt et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The melanopsin-mediated response of each ipRGC subtype differs in size, sensitivity, and kinetics.
source: Though all ipRGC subtypes require melanopsin phototransduction for intrinsic photosensitivity, the melanopsin-mediated response of each subtype differs in size, sensitivity, and kinetics and will differentially shape the visual information relayed to the brain (Graham et al., 2008; Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009; Ecker et al., 2010; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Estevez et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2018; Sonoda et al., 2018; Stabio et al., 2018; Quattrochi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Melanopsin shares greater sequence homology with invertebrate rhodopsins than vertebrate opsins.
source: Melanopsin shares greater sequence homology with invertebrate rhodopsins than vertebrate opsins, which led to an early expectation that melanopsin phototransduction in all ipRGC subtypes would work through an identical, invertebrate-like signaling pathway involving activation of a Gq/PLC-based cascade that opens canonical transient receptor potential (TRPC) channels such as TRPC 3, 6, or 7 (Provencio et al., 1998; Provencio et al., 2000; Koyanagi et al., 2005; Warren et al., 2006; Hartwick et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2008; Koyanagi and Terakita, 2008; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Graham et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: M1 ipRGCs use a Gq/PLC-based cascade to open only TRPC6/7 channels.
source: However, though M1 ipRGCs use this predicted Gq/PLC-based cascade to open only TRPC6/7 channels, phototransduction in non-M1 ipRGCs has been reported to rely less exclusively on TRPC channels and to also target additional channel types (Warren et al., 2006; Hartwick et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2011; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Sonoda et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2018; Contreras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Phototransduction in non-M1 ipRGCs relies less exclusively on TRPC channels and also targets additional channel types.
source: However, though M1 ipRGCs use this predicted Gq/PLC-based cascade to open only TRPC6/7 channels, phototransduction in non-M1 ipRGCs has been reported to rely less exclusively on TRPC channels and to also target additional channel types (Warren et al., 2006; Hartwick et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2011; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Sonoda et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2018; Contreras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In M2 cells, melanopsin phototransduction is reported to open both TRPC channels and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels.
source: In M2 cells, for example, melanopsin phototransduction is reported to open both TRPC channels and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2018; Contreras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research, though this claim is later contradicted by the current study's findings.

claim: Previous findings in M4 cells point to closure of potassium leak channels by melanopsin phototransduction and a minor contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channel opening.
source: Our previous findings in M4 cells point to closure of potassium leak channels by melanopsin phototransduction and a minor contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channel opening, while a concurrent study concluded that melanopsin phototransduction leads to opening of HCN channels in M4 cells with no contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channels (Sonoda et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2018; reviewed in Contreras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: A concurrent study concluded that melanopsin phototransduction leads to opening of HCN channels in M4 cells with no contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channels.
source: Our previous findings in M4 cells point to closure of potassium leak channels by melanopsin phototransduction and a minor contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channel opening, while a concurrent study concluded that melanopsin phototransduction leads to opening of HCN channels in M4 cells with no contribution from TRPC3/6/7 channels (Sonoda et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2018; reviewed in Contreras et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research by Jiang et al., 2018.

claim: TRPC3/6/7 channels contribute to M4 phototransduction in bright light.
source: To begin to resolve these discrepancies, we first recorded the M4 photocurrent under conditions that matched those used in Jiang et al. as closely as possible (Table 1 and see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing a significant decrease in the Early component amplitude in TRPC3/6/7 KO M4 cells (Figure 1D).

claim: Control M4 cells consistently exhibited an inward photocurrent that was composed of both a relatively fast, transient component followed by a slower, larger inward current that persisted for more than 30 s after termination of the 50 ms light pulse.
source: Control M4 cells consistently exhibited an inward photocurrent that was composed of both a relatively fast, transient component followed by a slower, larger inward current that persisted for more than 30 s after termination of the 50 ms light pulse (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The Early component of TRPC3/6/7 KO M4 ipRGCs is significantly reduced compared to Control.
source: The Early component of TRPC3/6/7 KO M4 ipRGCs is significantly reduced compared to Control (*p=0.0424).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Early, transient component of M4 photocurrent is largely driven by TRPC3/6/7 channels.
source: We found a significant decrease in the amplitude of the Early, transient, component in TRPC3/6/7 KO M4 cells, suggesting that this component is largely driven by TRPC3/6/7 channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing significant reduction in Early component in TRPC3/6/7 KO M4 cells (Figure 1D).

claim: Capacitance was not significantly different between control and TRPC3/6/7 M4 cells.
source: This was not due to changes in current density across genotypes because capacitance was not significantly different between control and TRPC3/6/7 M4 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Input resistance was similar across genotypes in M4 cells.
source: Input resistance was also similar across genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with 50 μM ZD7288 for 5–8 min was sufficient to eliminate the HCN tail current and achieve full HCN channel blockade in M4 ipRGCs.
source: We found that treatment with 50 μM ZD7288 for 5–8 min was sufficient to eliminate the HCN tail current and achieve full HCN channel blockade in M4 ipRGCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No reduction in the M4 photocurrent was observed in 50 μM ZD7288 despite elimination of the HCN tail current.
source: However, we observed no reduction in the M4 photocurrent in 50 μM ZD7288 despite elimination of the HCN tail current under these conditions (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: M4 ipRGCs express HCN channels, but HCN channels are not required for melanopsin phototransduction.
source: Thus, though M4 ipRGCs do express HCN channels, HCN channels are not required for melanopsin phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing HCN tail currents in M4 cells but no effect of HCN blockade on photocurrent (Figure 2).

claim: Light does not alter the amplitude of the M4 HCN current or tail current.
source: We found no change in either the M4 HCN current or tail current amplitudes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), indicating that light does not modulate the HCN current, further arguing against HCN involvement in M4 phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The reversal potential of the M4 HCN tail current is distinct from the reversal of the M4 photocurrent.
source: Unlike the I–V relationship of the M4 photocurrent reversal at –90 mV, the linear fit of the M4 HCN tail current shows an extrapolated reversal at –26 mV. Though consistent with the properties of HCN channels (Biel et al., 2009), the extrapolated M4 HCN tail current I–V reversal is distinct from the reversal of the M4 photocurrent (M4 photocurrent replotted in Figure 3B from Sonoda et al., 2018, see also Figures 7D and S6 of Sonoda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and comparison to previous data.

claim: Longer, 20 min incubation with 50 μM ZD7288 essentially abolished the M4 photocurrent and increased M4 cell input resistance compared to control.
source: Despite identical HCN channel blockade, this longer 20 min incubation with 50 μM ZD7288 now essentially abolished the M4 photocurrent and increased M4 cell input resistance compared to control (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: The M4 photocurrent blockade following longer incubations with ZD7288 was due to off-target effects.
source: These results are consistent with potential nonspecific blockade of potassium channels by ZD7288 and provide a methodological explanation for previous conclusions of HCN involvement in M4 phototransduction (Do and Bean, 2003; Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased input resistance and citations to previous research on ZD7288 off-target effects.

claim: 5–8 min incubation period with ZD7288 effectively blocked M2 HCN channels.
source: We then measured HCN tail currents in M2 cells before and after 5–8 min incubation with 50 μM ZD7288 and found that the HCN currents and tail currents were completely abolished under these conditions, identifying an effective concentration and incubation period of ZD7288 for full HCN channel blockade in M2 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HCN channel blockade with an effective concentration and incubation period of ZD7288 did not reduce the M2 photocurrent.
source: As with M4 cells, HCN channel blockade with an effective concentration and incubation period of ZD7288 did not reduce the M2 photocurrent (Figure 4D and E), suggesting that HCN channels are not a target of melanopsin phototransduction in M2 cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The M2 HCN current is not modulated by light.
source: Again, like M4 cells, we found no change in the amplitude of the M2 HCN tail current recorded in background light compared to darkness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), despite a steady, light-evoked inward current at the starting holding potential of –66 mV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E). This indicates that the M2 HCN current is not modulated by light.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: HCN channels, though expressed in M2 cells, are not a target of M2 melanopsin phototransduction.
source: This further supports the conclusion that HCN channels, though expressed in M2 cells, are not a target of M2 melanopsin phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of HCN blockade on M2 photocurrent and no light modulation of HCN current.

claim: The additional photocurrent blockade observed with longer ZD7288 incubation was due to off-target effects on non-HCN channels in M2 cells.
source: These findings suggest that this additional photocurrent blockade observed in this study and in previous work was due to off-target effects on non-HCN channels in M2 cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no additional HCN blockade but photocurrent reduction with longer incubation, and citations to previous research on ZD7288 off-target effects.

claim: The maximum amplitude was reduced by ~75% in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs, and the Early component was essentially completely abolished.
source: We found that the maximum amplitude was reduced by ~75% in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs, and the Early component was essentially completely abolished (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Capacitance and resistance were identical in TRPC3/6/7 KO and Control M2 Cells.
source: This was not due to changes in intrinsic properties because capacitance and resistance were identical in TRPC3/6/7 KO and Control M2 Cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No further reduction in the small remaining photocurrent of TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 was observed following 5–8 min incubation with the HCN antagonist ZD7288 (50 μM).
source: Additionally, we observed no further reduction in the small remaining photocurrent of TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 following 5–8 min incubation with the HCN antagonist ZD7288 (50 μM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The HCN tail current and inward current were not significantly altered by light exposure in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs.
source: Furthermore, both the HCN tail current and inward current were not significantly altered by light exposure in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: There is no evidence of HCN involvement in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs.
source: Thus, as with WT M2 phototransduction, we find no evidence of HCN involvement in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 ipRGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of HCN blockade and no light modulation of HCN current in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells.

claim: All photocurrent components in control M2 ipRGCs reversed between +10 mV and +25 mV.
source: All photocurrent components in control M2 ipRGCs reversed between +10 mV and +25 mV, suggesting contributions from cation channels that are more permeable to sodium or calcium, such as TRPC channels (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In TRPC3/6/7 KO retinas, I–V relationships reversed between 0 mV and +10 mV.
source: In TRPC3/6/7 KO retinas, I–V relationships reversed between 0 mV and +10 mV, and the Maximum, Intermediate, and Late component amplitudes were reduced at more hyperpolarized, physiologically relevant, potentials while the Early component was reduced at all potentials (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HCN tail currents in M2 ipRGCs reversed at –32 mV, which is distinct from that of the photocurrent reversal at +19 mV for control and ~0 mV for TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells.
source: Notably, HCN tail currents in M2 ipRGCs reversed at –32 mV, which is distinct from that of the photocurrent reversal at +19 mV for control and ~0 mV for TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells (Figure 7A and B), further arguing against HCN involvement in M2 phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The I–V relationship of M1 and M2 ipRGCs differed in shape and reversal potential, with M1 cells having a more linear I–V relationship that reverses at 0 mV compared to a more complex I–V relationship that reverses +19 mV for M2 cells.
source: However, we observed that the I–V relationship of M1 and M2 ipRGCs differed in shape and reversal potential, with M1 cells having a more linear I–V relationship that reverses at 0 mV compared to a more complex I–V relationship that reverses +19 mV for M2 cells (Figure 8A; Warren et al., 2006; Hartwick et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2011; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Sonoda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A and citations to previous research.

claim: Application of VGCC antagonists resulted in a significant reduction of the overall M2 photocurrent similar to that seen in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells.
source: Application of VGCC antagonists resulted in a significant reduction of the overall M2 photocurrent similar to that seen in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells, indicating that VGCCs are required for M2 melanopsin phototransduction (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: VGCC blockade did not reduce the M1 photocurrent.
source: Importantly, VGCC blockade did not reduce the M1 photocurrent (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: VGCCs are not required for melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs.
source: This indicates that VGCCs are not required for melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs and that VGCCs may account for some of the observed differences in the M1 versus M2 photocurrent I–V relationships.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of VGCC blockade on M1 photocurrent (Figure 8D and E).

claim: T-type VGCC mRNA expression has been reported in M2 ipRGCs.
source: T-type VGCC mRNA expression has been reported in M2 ipRGCs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A; Tran et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research and data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: T-type VGCC immunolabeling is detected in ON-stratifying ipRGCs in retinal sections.
source: and we detect T-type VGCC immunolabeling in ON-stratifying ipRGCs in retinal sections (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TTA-P2 reduced M2 current amplitudes, and TTA-P2-sensitive currents showed I–V relationships consistent with T-type VGCC channels.
source: We found that TTA-P2 reduced M2 current amplitudes in this protocol, and that TTA-P2-sensitive currents showed I–V relationships consistent with T-type VGCC channels (Wu et al., 2018; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Randall and Tsien, 1997; Monteil et al., 2000; Fox et al., 1987; Dreyfus et al., 2010; Choe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A and citations to previous research.

claim: M2 ipRGCs express functional T-type VGCC channels.
source: Combined, these data provide evidence that M2 ipRGCs express functional T-type VGCC channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing T-type VGCC currents in M2 cells (Figure 9A).

claim: T-type blockade nearly eliminates the M2 photocurrent without reducing the HCN tail current.
source: We found that T-type blockade nearly eliminates the M2 photocurrent without reducing the HCN tail current (Figure 9B and C, Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and C, and Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: The M2 photocurrent was similarly reduced in the presence of a second T-type VGCC antagonist, mibefradil (10 µM).
source: The M2 photocurrent was similarly reduced in the presence of a second T-type VGCC antagonist, mibefradil (10 µM) (Figure 10), suggesting that T-type VGCCs are required for melanopsin phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Mibefradil had no effect on the M2 photocurrent in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells.
source: Importantly, mibefradil had no effect on the M2 photocurrent in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells (Figure 10), suggesting that TRPC 3/6/7 channels and T-type channels act through a common pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: TRPC 3/6/7 channels and T-type channels act through a common pathway in M2 cells.
source: Importantly, mibefradil had no effect on the M2 photocurrent in TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells (Figure 10), suggesting that TRPC 3/6/7 channels and T-type channels act through a common pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no additional reduction of photocurrent when TRPC3/6/7 KO M2 cells were treated with mibefradil (Figure 10).

claim: A VGCC cocktail lacking T-type antagonists did not significantly reduce the M2 photocurrent.
source: We next recorded the M2 photocurrent in a cocktail of VGCC antagonists that did not contain T-type antagonists (see 'Materials and methods'). This VGCC cocktail lacking T-type antagonists did not significantly reduce the M2 photocurrent (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), further supporting a role for T-type VGCCs in M2 phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: TTA-P2 alone had no effect on the M1 photocurrent.
source: As with the full VGCC cocktail used above, TTA-P2 alone had no effect on the M1 photocurrent (Figure 9D and E), suggesting that VGCCs are dispensable for M1 phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: The complete lack of blockade of the M1 photocurrent by TTA-P2 or the VGCC antagonist cocktail argues against reduction of the M2 photocurrent resulting from nonspecific effects of these drugs on TRPC channels.
source: Importantly, this complete lack of blockade of the M1 photocurrent by TTA-P2 or the VGCC antagonist cocktail also argues against reduction of the M2 photocurrent resulting from nonspecific effects of these drugs on TRPC channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect on M1 photocurrent (Figure 8D and E, Figure 9D and E).

claim: T-type VGCCs play a key, previously unappreciated, role in M2, but not M1, melanopsin phototransduction.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest a key, previously unappreciated, role for T-type VGCCs in M2, but not M1, melanopsin phototransduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing T-type VGCC blockade eliminates M2 but not M1 photocurrent.

claim: Melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs opens TRPC 3/6/7 channels.
source: While melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs opens TRPC 3/6/7 channels, in M2 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction requires both TRPC and T-type VGCCs, and in M4 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction closes leak potassium channels.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and experimental data from this study.

claim: In M2 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction requires both TRPC and T-type VGCCs.
source: While melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs opens TRPC 3/6/7 channels, in M2 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction requires both TRPC and T-type VGCCs, and in M4 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction closes leak potassium channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study showing TRPC and T-type VGCC involvement in M2 phototransduction.

claim: In M4 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction closes leak potassium channels.
source: While melanopsin phototransduction in M1 ipRGCs opens TRPC 3/6/7 channels, in M2 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction requires both TRPC and T-type VGCCs, and in M4 ipRGCs melanopsin phototransduction closes leak potassium channels.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and experimental data from this study.

claim: In M4 ipRGCs, closure of potassium channels increases the excitability of M4 cells, enhancing cellular (and likely behavioral) contrast sensitivity.
source: For example, in M4 ipRGCs, closure of potassium channels increases the excitability of M4 cells, enhancing cellular (and likely behavioral) contrast sensitivity while M1 ipRGCs perform simpler luminance-detecting functions to impact behaviors that integrate luminance information across long timescales (Berson et al., 2002; Hattar et al., 2002; Ruby et al., 2002; Lucas et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2005; Güler et al., 2008; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Wong, 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014; Emanuel and Do, 2015; Sonoda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: M1 ipRGCs perform simpler luminance-detecting functions to impact behaviors that integrate luminance information across long timescales.
source: For example, in M4 ipRGCs, closure of potassium channels increases the excitability of M4 cells, enhancing cellular (and likely behavioral) contrast sensitivity while M1 ipRGCs perform simpler luminance-detecting functions to impact behaviors that integrate luminance information across long timescales (Berson et al., 2002; Hattar et al., 2002; Ruby et al., 2002; Lucas et al., 2003; Wong et al., 2005; Güler et al., 2008; Perez-Leighton et al., 2011; Wong, 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014; Emanuel and Do, 2015; Sonoda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both male and female mice were used with a mixed B6/129 background.
source: Both male and female mice were used with a mixed B6/129 background.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: All mice were between 30 and 90 d of age.
source: All mice were between 30 and 90 d of age.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: M4 ipRGCs are synonymous with ON-sustained alpha RGCs.
source: M4 ipRGCs, synonymous with ON-sustained alpha RGCs (Schmidt et al., 2014), were identified in IR-DIC as cells with large somata (>20 μm) and characteristic ON-sustained responses to increments in light, as described in Sonoda et al., 2018.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: M4 ipRGCs were identified in IR-DIC as cells with large somata (>20 μm) and characteristic ON-sustained responses to increments in light.
source: M4 ipRGCs, synonymous with ON-sustained alpha RGCs (Schmidt et al., 2014), were identified in IR-DIC as cells with large somata (>20 μm) and characteristic ON-sustained responses to increments in light, as described in Sonoda et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell identification criteria.

claim: The identity of M4 ipRGCs was confirmed by verifying the dendrites stratified only in the ON-sublamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) and immunolabeled with SMI-32.
source: After all cellular recordings, the identity of M4 ipRGCs was confirmed by verifying the dendrites stratified only in the ON-sublamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) and immunolabeled with SMI-32, an M4 ipRGC marker (Schmidt et al., 2014; Sonoda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell identification criteria, supported by citations.

claim: M2 cell dendrites stratified only in the ON-sublamina of the IPL while M1 cell dendrites stratified in the OFF-sublamina of the IPL.
source: M2 cell dendrites stratified only in the ON-sublamina of the IPL while M1 cell dendrites stratified in the OFF-sublamina of the IPL (described in Schmidt et al., 2008 and Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell identification criteria, supported by citations.

claim: Both M1 and M2 were confirmed negative for SMI-32 immunolabeling.
source: Both M1 and M2 were confirmed negative for SMI-32 immunolabeling as described in Lee and Schmidt, 2018.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell identification criteria, supported by citation.
